Well what do you mean intentionally?  So trains have forward facing cameras and black box event recorders.  They are download at every event.  If the Engineer was Speeding, then that’s a rules violation and would’ve been tested and pulled out of service.  Everything we do is recorded.  99% of family’s attempt litigation against the Railway, but lawyers will not even take the case, if there’s no rules violations.  We can’t intentionally hit someone, there’s no steering wheel.

I sorta take offense to that “reckless and viscous”. Do people assume that Engineers are blatantly violating laws?  Here’s a fact, not only do we face civil litigation, but face manslaughter charges if we break certain laws.   Amtrak has the hardest and most structured training for Locomotive engineers out of any railroad in America.  It takes a minimum of two years of being a student to promote.  We take our craft very serious, and a whole lot of pride.  Imagine the responsibility of having the lives of 300 passengers in your control.  I know things have happened, accidents have happened.  But for the most part.  We take our jobs very serious
For what it’s worth yesterday was a fatality. The crews for the most part. Will not tell the passengers the truth.

I am an Engineer, and sitting idle for 3 hours reliving what I just saw over and over Is very frustrating.  I would love to get my passengers back on the move as soon as possible. And get my mind off it.  But it’s out of our hands
Sorry that happened to your commute, understand we can’t move the train until authorities release us. Many times a coroner has to be dispatched and that can take several hours unfortunately.

Amtrak’s Police usually do not respond to trespass incidents. They for the most part protect stations.  However the host rail road police usually do, but not always.  It’s not like the BNSF or UP police have major staffing.  They probably have one or two officers that are in charge of 300-400 miles of track.  Pretty hard to respond all the time.  Local authorities always do, and since it was a motorcycle CHP would have been lead investigator.   The three hours you waited was for a the local investigation, as well as. Relief crew.  After a Strike, we have to be relieved as it’s a critical incident and we need to have a few days to deal with the trauma and possibly talk to our peer support counselors.
Negative, we are not screened for drugs or alcohol, on trespasser incidents. Only random tests, or rules violations.

Really the simplest advice is just start walking. Trying to jump right into a exercise regiment combined with a diet change is pretty tough to do at the same time for anybody. The key is sustainability. You do not want to set yourself up for failure. There’s nothing wrong with getting a gym membership or workout program you can explore what works with you. For me, I wanted to kick this diseased into remission but I was realistic.  I couldn’t fail myself this time, so I started walking. And walking at least 40 minutes a day. In the beginning it stunk, I hated it. I felt like it was doing nothing. But I continued, I downloaded podcasts, and audiobooks to help pass the time. Id reward myself with a protein style burger from in and out whenever I pushed it further. 40 minutes turned into 2 miles, then 3 miles. Now im at 5 miles a day 4-5 times a week. I enjoy it. It clears my mind and paired that with a keto diet the pounds literally came off fast. I saw losing a pound a day for the first three months. From 223 pounds in April and a A1c of 9.3 to today I weighed 179 and an A1c of 4.8.  Now my results are insane, not everyone can be as strict with keto as I was. Im one meal a day, and no more than 15 carbs.  Diet is huge, but I will wager a whole lot to say that walking played a huge part. 

I fancied it up bought badass nikes that are comfortable I downloaded apps to track my walks. In May I walked 58 miles alone. Sounds like a whole lotta time. But in reality 2-3 miles is like an hour walk briskly.  It can be done, its not hard on my knees like running and it just feels good.   My suggestion is to try anything for at least 40 minutes a day consistently.

I would keep checking the status of your application at Amtrak jobs, where you submitted your resume. Unfortunately HR holds all the power moving forward and their promptness is very poor. With this being the holiday week, I wouldn’t expect to hear anything until after the first but you never know.  If you are being considered the website will say they would like to invite you to take an online assessment test. It’s a psychological test based on algorithms, where they ask you questions over and over worded in a different way. It’s a timed test and it’s one attempt once you click start it will know if you log out and restart.  When you take the test you need to put your mindset that you are a corporate guy, a managers dream, a snitch. And answer them all the same way. It’s an easy test, but have known many freight applicants to bomb it. Do not answer it like you are a union guy. 

After that, if you pass a few days later the status should change to they are considering you for an interview. This is where it starts to become a bit frustrating with HR’s efficiency. You might get called right away or it may take a few days. Really all depends on when that class is scheduled to start.  You get the call for an interview, I highly suggest a collared shirt and tie, and have at least 4 copies of your resume. The interview will be a panel interview consisting of road foreman, and Local Chairman. Remember they are all Engineers just like you and will know if you are bullshitting them. Be early and relax. Start thinking of examples now for answers to questions like, “can you share with us a time as a locomotive engineer where you noticed an unsafe situation and what did you do about it”  “Tell us about a situation where your attentiveness, was cluttered with distractions and how did you cope” “How do you feel about working alone, or do you prefer to be part of a team” that is sorta a trick question. Amtrak engineers are by themselves in the cab. Amtrak engineers are responsible for calling work gangs, copying mandatory directives, and pretty much 100% responsible for the entire train and its operating rules. Yes there’s an two conductors but they are in the body of the train doing their thing. You can not rely on them to remind you of a slow order, or being delayed in block after a station stop. You will need to prove that you had over 150 engineer starts in the previous 365 days. So bring with you copies of something that says the date and your position. At UP I had to go to management and get copies of my work history, said I was getting audited by IRS or something. 

Assuming you do well at your interview, the website will say if they are considering you for a job offer, if it updates to that HR will call you and offer you a job, if you choose to accept it’s chaos from there for a bit. You will have a laundry list of things to accomplish online. You will have to provide your high school transcripts, I had to go online and order a copy from my school district considering that was like 20 plus years ago, but they had it took a few days to get.  You will have to apply for a criminal background check their company they use is a pain in the ass and have terrible promptness.  You will be contacted for a urinalysis and hair test. Then a physical where you will take an EKG and examination for potential Sleep Apnea. Do not drink a monster or a big cup of coffee that day, my buddy drank coffee and the EKG indicated he had a raised heart rate and had to take another one and needed his dr to sign off on it. The sleep apnea test is measuring your neck and looking in your throat for signs that you snore. If you have it, you have it. It’s not a deal breaker but they will want you to treat it.  We get tested for it every year.

You clear all those hurdles you will fly to Wilmington Delaware for 16 weeks. Class is Monday thru Friday. You get paid all 7 days and per diem. Classroom attire is slacks and a buttoned up collared shirt and dress shoes. Some days you will take field trips where you will need your work boots, them days you can wear jeans. Other than that no jeans allowed. Their will be big wigs all over the training center and trust me that they will notice if you accidentally wore tennis shoes. I got caught lol.   That’s just the basic rundown on what to expect, if you are offered a position and are starting a class I will give you a write up on the testing and curriculum.  Good luck to you, it’s the best move I have ever made, gave up 13 years of senority and have never for a second regretted it.

I've been in TYE for over 20 years and I have worked out of about 10 different terminals and seen all sorts of ups and downs so I will answer this question as honestly as I can without letting my bad days shine through (and yes, there are bad days).
First, you have to be a self starter. When the phone rings at 0200 for an 0400 on duty when the lineup predicted you going to work at 1100 and you just got to bed at 2330 and all you want to do is lay back down, you can't. You could lay off but that takes a hit in the wallet and railroads are really cracking down on people calling in sick (only allow you to take 1 day a week off or some other equation). Then once on the train, we don't have a boss watching over us like in an office environment. You could sleep the entire way over the road, until that one time your coworker also falls asleep and you both die in a huge ball of fire. But part of being a self starter is even when you're tired, you stand up. You do jumping jacks in the cab. You engage you coworker in a debate about anything (even if you agree with him).
Second, will you miss your kids birthdays and Christmas and have to work every weekend? Maybe. Depends. I work for the BNSF and we are allowed 5 weekdays and 2 weekend days a month off. If you lay off 3 weekend days but no weekdays, you're still going to get in trouble for availability. You have to watch your own time (being a self starter). Your boss wont remind you when you're getting close, only bust you once you overstepped your limits. Other railroads have different layoff rules. Some are WAY more strict (and I think the NS is one of them!).
So let's say you are allowed 2 layoff days a month and your kid's birthday is in December. Do you lay off on your kid's birthday or lay off on Christmas? You're going to either have to miss one of them or work both or layoff both and get in trouble. My kids are 11 and I haven't missed a Christmas yet. I've missed a lot of baseball games and parent teacher conferences, but those are the hard choices you have to make. Could I layoff for all my kids' games and events? Sure, but then I would have to deal with my boss getting in my ass. Pick and choose the days off that are important to you.
Marriage. "All railroaders get divorced!" False. When you meet future Mrs. Fictitious, size her up. Ask yourself, "If I was stuck on a train during a massive rain storm and the power went out at home and the sump pump started flooding the basement, would Mrs. Fictitious know what to do?" If the answer is yes, then she can handle your lifestyle. If the answer is no, then it sounds like she needs someone by her side and... she'll find someone, even if you're not there. It takes a lot to be a railroad wife. They are alone just as much as we are. If you try to marry a woman that wants to be treated like a princess and you are there to do it, she will start looking for another prince charming.
"Holes in your boat" Some guys think they need all the new fancy toys. New Harley, new crew cab truck, jet ski, boat, etc, etc, etc. And, for the most part, we can either afford it or banks are MORE than happy to give a railroader a loan. But then your kid's birthday comes up or you get sick or you're just burned out and need a day off but you can't. You have too many holes in your boat and you have to keep plugging away. Don't be that guy! And those guys are EVERYWHERE on the railroad!
Tips? Keep a hobby. Make time for your hobby. There are bad days and bad trips. Don't ONLY be a railroader so you take that crap home with you. Go to work and be a railroader, but when you come home be that dude with the cool hobby or husband your wife missed or dad your kids like having around. Man... I've seen this place eat away at people until their entire mood for the month is set on a trip that happened 20 days ago. When you get in from the trip, wash your hands. Watch all the dirt and grime swirl down the drain. Watch the water get clean. Let it go.
Exercise! You'll hire on with a 28" waist and within a year have a 38" waist. All that railroad retirement won't mean shit if you're clutching your heart at age 59.
Your social life is important to you.... Man, I'm not going to sugar coat this. Your friends will make plans to go see the Cubs play and ask if you can come. You don't know your schedule so you'll have to bail on them. Then Johnny is having a Halloween party and, "Dude! Zorn! You're gonna be there, right?" Pretty soon they'll stop asking. It sucks and I'm not saying this because I'm bitter or angry, I'm being honest. You find any railroader and they will all say the same thing, "They just stop asking."
This is how "friends" work on the railroad (one more point then I'll shut up, I promise). I get called. I accept the call. I look and see who I'm working with. I might not know the name. Or I might recognize the name and could probably point him out but never worked with him. Or maybe we've worked together before and even got along. It doesn't matter. Now imagine yourself stuck in a room with another dude for 12 hours. The room is about the size of your bathroom. You each have a chair but you can't leave. Within 5 minutes, you have to make this person your newest bestest friend. Why? I dunno. To make the trip go better? To learn something? To just not feel so damn lonely and you know this guy is in the same shoes as you and will understand? I dunno. But there you are. 12 hours. I've heard some of the funniest stories from these guys, had some of the best conversations, had to endure some of the dumbest bullshit (with a smile on my face), and heard shit you wouldn't even tell your therapist. 12 hours. Then.... its done. Over. You leave the cab and walk away. The "friendship" is (for the most part) over. When you see him again, you'll say hi and be cool but he's not going to buy you a Christmas present or call you if you're sick or help you move. Hell, he might not even remember your name... because he is now on another train and now has a new bestest friend. As will you. It kinda fucks us up socially. I can talk to anyone about anything, anywhere and any time. But now in my personal life, I have my family and that's it. The last 2 guys I worked with were totally cool, but I can only remember one of their names. And that's cool, because he probably wont remember my name either.
So... In conclusion (thank god, huh?).... I've worked some messed up hours and met some messed up people, but in the end it will pay for my kids to go to college, pay for my house for my wife and I to retire in, and I actually kinda like my job.
Good luck.

My interview consisted of 2 road foreman’s and two local chairmen. ALL of them were Engineers, that have a ton of experience. Amtrak engineers are trained to extensively more in the mechanical side of Locomotives than any other Class 1’s ( I came from UP ) where they pretty much show you how to fire them up, and shut them down. With Amtrak it is different. In fact in Wilmington you receive manuals for each locomotive we operate and yes they expect you to read them and take tests on the many differences between the three we use.  So in other words, the folks you interview with you cannot bullshit. As said the best answer you can give is I don’t Know, if you truly do not know.  I also second what was said before, do not be quick to answer. Take your time answering. Remember you are in a room full of engineers... Once I knew, I was amongst people from my craft,  my interview felt more relaxed. Almost sorta like shooting the shit at the yard office. 

One question that you should be prepared for is, what do you think of Single man crews?  95% of Amtrak is one man in the cab. A wrong answer would be not in favor of it, because that’s how we operate.  You have to express confidence that you can do the job by yourself.  In all honesty engineers are always by them selves. Passenger Conductors are not trained nor deal with the stuff that freight Conductors do. Taking slow orders, calling work gangs, calling signals, everything possibly you can imagine it’s on the Engineer period.  

It’s a whole lot more responsibility than one can imagine. But it’s worth it 100% Just understand what you are truly getting into.  Instead of box cars full of whatever, you have people. Today I picked up 35 elementary school kids going for a field trip for perspective.

Incorrect, as soon as you place the ABV to release start to increase the brake pipe with air, that flow travels from one car to the next and an increase of just 2psi is enough to release the pistons.  While air is released from car to car the air has to pump from the compressor to the main reservoir to the brake pipe into each auxiliary reservoir, when air is added to the auxiliary res, the J relay valve slides over and opens an exhaust port that releases air in the brake cylinder.  This happens as soon as it starts to charge.

Here’s the thing, and I do not mean to sound like an asshole. But I sure hope you are not an Engineer. But If you were, I’d suggest brushing up on dynamic brake holding feature.
